definition: To keep refining an instruction past the point of improvement; to polish a working prompt until it breaks.
etymology: Back-formed from overwrought (‘overworked; agitated’) on the maker-suffix -wright — and deliberately a homophone of computing’s overwrite, because over-editing destroys the version that worked. Three words fold into one, and every maker knows the fault the moment they hear it.
in_use: It ran fine three versions ago. Then I overwrighted it.
the_case: The prompt was working — that is what makes this one dangerous. Over-instructing is harder to catch than its opposite because it wears the mask of diligence: under-instructing feels like laziness and you notice it, while adding one more clause feels like care, and nobody flinches at care. Naming the fault turns it into craft — the sound of a maker recognising the moment to put the tool down and step back from the bench.
